articles.title: A South African farmer planted trees to stop erosion in 1976; 50 years later, the land became a major forest-restoration experiment
articles.summary: Rest of World News: A small planting on a South African farm in 1976 was meant to solve an immediate problem: stopping floodwater from washing away soil and threatening l.
articles.body: A small planting on a South African farm in 1976 was meant to solve an immediate problem: stopping floodwater from washing away soil and threatening livestock. The spekboom cuttings survived, but their story did not end there. More than four decades later, the same hillside had become a valuable example of how degraded land can begin to recover. Other vegetation returned, wildlife followed and scientists found evidence of changes beneath the soil as well. The old planting would eventually help shape a much larger restoration experiment across the Eastern Cape, where millions of spekboom cuttings were tested as a way to rebuild damaged landscapes.The 1976 planting that quietly transformed a damaged hillsideAccording to Global Issues, the planting took place in 1976 in the Kromport area of the Eastern Cape. Behind a farm barn was a steep slope, roughly 200 metres by 100 metres, where erosion and recurring floods had become a problem.The farmer planted cuttings of spekboom (Portulacaria afra), hoping the vegetation would slow the movement of water and protect his livestock. The cuttings established themselves on the degraded ground, and the flooding problem eased. What mattered later was that the plants were left in place.Some of the spekboom plants eventually became more than 40 years old. Other vegetation began to appear around them, while birds and wildlife returned to an area that had previously been heavily disturbed.Spekboom’s unusual traits make it suited to restorationSpekboom is a succulent native to South Africa. It has fleshy leaves and stems that allow it to cope with dry conditions, while its ability to grow from cuttings makes it relatively straightforward to propagate.That combination is useful in the Eastern Cape, where water can be scarce and degraded soils can be difficult places for plants to establish. As spekboom grows, it produces leaves that eventually fall and add organic material to the soil. Its roots contribute to the accumulation of carbon below ground, while the vegetation itself stores carbon.In mountainous areas, spekboom can grow on slopes and help slow runoff when rain arrives. Rather than allowing water to rush across bare ground and carry soil into rivers, vegetation gives some of that water a chance to soak into the landscape.How centuries of grazing changed the Eastern Cape landscapeThe significance of the experiment becomes clearer when looking at what once covered much of the Eastern Cape.Spekboom is a dominant component of the region's subtropical thicket, a dense and diverse vegetation system that historically covered millions of hectares across the dry parts of the province.Much of that landscape was gradually degraded through intensive grazing, particularly by goats and sheep. Vegetation was removed faster than it could recover, leaving large areas exposed and increasingly vulnerable to erosion.Land that had once supported a dense thicket became much more open, with only scattered remnants of the original vegetation surviving. Jacket plum trees were among the species that could still be found in some degraded areas, providing clues about the ecosystem that had previously existed there.Ecologists studying the region estimated that more than 1.3 million hectares of severely degraded thicket could potentially be restored.The old Kromport planting offered an important clue about how that might be done.A 40-year-old experiment changed the questionThe remarkable thing about the original planting was not simply that the spekboom had survived.Other plants began returning. Wildlife came back. The vegetation started to resemble parts of the thicket that had once occupied the area. For scientists, the site offered something difficult to obtain through a conventional experiment: time.A restoration project lasting a few years can show whether plants survive. A site that has been growing for four decades can reveal much more about what happens afterwards.Scientists were able to examine carbon held in the plants, their roots and the surrounding soil. They could also observe changes in the wider vegetation community.The small farm site therefore became a reference point for a much larger question: could spekboom be used to help restore extensive areas of degraded thicket?The experiment showed that planting was only the first stepIn 2007, the South African government began establishing hundreds of demonstration plots across degraded thicket areas.Around 330 plots, each covering half a hectare, were planted with spekboom across a vast area of the Eastern Cape. The aim was to test whether the plant could establish itself under different environmental conditions and with different planting techniques. It was one of the country's largest ecological restoration experiments.The results were encouraging, but they also showed that simply putting cuttings into the ground was not enough.Young spekboom plants needed protection from goats and other livestock while they became established. Fencing for several years could make the difference between a planting surviving and disappearing again. The lesson was fairly straightforward: restoration depended as much on protecting young vegetation as on choosing the right plant.A farmer eventually faced the same problemMore than 30 years after the first spekboom planting, another South African farmer was confronting the consequences of degraded land.Pieter Kruger owned Zandvlakte in the Bavianskloof. His farm had suffered from erosion and vegetation loss, while water had become increasingly difficult to find.The situation eventually forced Kruger to abandon goat farming and take a different approach. He joined the government's Working for Water programme, which was involved in restoring degraded landscapes and watersheds.Over the next three years, about 1,500 hectares of his farm were planted with millions of spekboom cuttings. More than 100 workers were involved in the restoration work.Restored vegetation helped the farm withstand a major floodThe restored vegetation was put to the test during a major flood. Instead of water simply racing across the surface, the vegetation helped slow the runoff. More water could penetrate the soil, reducing the amount of topsoil being carried away.For Kruger, this was a practical demonstration of what restoration could mean on a working farm.The land was not being restored as an isolated nature reserve. It still had to function economically.His property later expanded into ecotourism, giving visitors an opportunity to see the restored landscape while creating another source of income.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: IT giants' PERM filings suspended: What does this mean for Green Card applicants?
articles.summary: US News: Thousands of foreign technology workers hoping to secure US Green Cards through employer sponsorship are facing fresh uncertainty after the US Departm.
articles.body: Thousands of foreign technology workers hoping to secure US Green Cards through employer sponsorship are facing fresh uncertainty after the US Department of Labor suspended PERM filings by IT services giant Cognizant and software company Cloudera amid an investigation into alleged fraud and misuse of employment-based visa programmes. Department of Labor's Inspector General Anthony D'Esposito announced the action on social media and also spoke about their investigation preceding the action on Texas journalist Sara Gonzales's show. Calling it a huge deal, D'Esposito said American people will finally see that "we are for real".Gonzales described Cognizant as a massive hirer of foreign labor and cited data that the company had 41,571 beneficiaries for H-1B approval only in Texas in 2025.There has been no official USCIS or DOL announcement to this effect. No details have been revealed yet and D'Esposito's social media posts led to some confusion as he mentioned PERM filings and H-1B processings both which are very different from each other.What is PERM and why does it matter?PERM is the Department of Labor's labour-certification process through which an employer generally has to demonstrate that there are no qualified and available US workers for a particular job and that employing a foreign worker will not adversely affect the wages and working conditions of similarly employed US workers.For a typical employer-sponsored EB-2 or EB-3 Green Card case, the process can broadly look like this:PERM → I-140 → priority date becomes current → Green CardThat means a worker who has not yet reached the PERM filing stage could face a delay in starting the Green Card process if the employer is unable to submit a new application.Existing Green Card holders not believed to be impactedThe suspension of new PERM filings does not, by itself, mean that every existing Green Card case of these two companies has been cancelled.An employee who has not yet started PERM is likely to face a different situation from someone whose PERM has already been approved and whose I-140 has subsequently been filed or approved. Similarly, someone who already has a Green Card or another independently valid immigration status is not automatically affected simply because their employer is under investigation.Is H-1B processing related to this?The PERM suspension and an individual's H-1B status are separate immigration matters. An investigation into an employer does not automatically cancel the H-1B status of every employee working for that company. The worker's individual petition, status and circumstances remain important.While Cognizant is an Indian-American company, Cloudera is a fully American company.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: ‘Making memes’: P Chidambaram says Gen Z is having last laugh over PM Modi’s ‘naraaz fufa’ jibe
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Former Union minister and Congress leader P Chidambaram on Wednesday hit back at Prime Minister Narendra Modi over his recent remarks targe.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Former Union minister and Congress leader P Chidambaram on Wednesday hit back at Prime Minister Narendra Modi over his recent remarks targeting the Opposition, saying he was “happy” and “proud” to be called a “Dimagi Naxal” and describing the “Naraaz Fufa” remark as meaningless.Speaking to news agency ANI, Chidambaram said, “I'm happy that I'm not a Bewakoof Naxal. I'm happy that I am a Dimagi Naxal.”Calling PM Modi a “self-confessed poet”, Chidambaram said the Prime Minister often coins slogans and expressions and later translates them into English.“He is a self-confessed poet. He writes poetry in Gujarati. I think he coins these words in Gujarati and translates them into English. I read the translation into English, but this is his way,” Chidambaram said.“He started by saying, ‘acche din aane wale hain’. Then I counted the slogans he had coined. I think there are something like 20-25 slogans in the last 12 years. The latest two are the ‘Dimagi Naxal’ and ‘Naraaz Fufa’,” he added.Chidambaram says Gen Z has turned remarks into memesChidambaram said PM Modi's remarks had generated discussion on social media, particularly among Gen Z users.“Tomorrow, he will say something. At the Brics Summit, he will say something. But these are meaningless. I am told that Gen Z has made a lot of memes on ‘Naraaz Fufa’ and ‘Dimagi Naxal’. When I tweeted that I'm proud to be a Dimagi Naxal, the likes were 5.5 million,” he said.“I don't know whether all of them claim to be Dimagi Naxals, but at least a substantial number of them liked the tweet, which means they are also Dimagi Naxals,” he added.Chidambaram had earlier reacted to PM Modi's “Dimagi Naxal” remarks in a post on X, writing, “I am proud to be a dimagi naxal!”PM Modi’s ‘Dimagi Naxal’ remarkChidambaram's comments came after PM Modi, in his Independence Day address from the Red Fort, urged people and authorities to “identify and isolate” those with a “dimagi naxal” or ideological Naxal mindset.The Prime Minister said government action since 2014 had largely ended jungle insurgency, which had claimed the lives of more than 3,500 security personnel. He also alleged that people with a “Maoist mentality” had earlier held positions in government committees and influenced policy.PM Modi said armed Maoist violence was “breathing its last”, but an ideological Naxal mindset continued to exist in some institutions. He also warned against allowing such a mindset to influence the country's youth.‘Naraaz Fufa’ jibe over freight corridorThe Congress leader's remarks also came a day after PM Modi revived his “Naraaz Fufa” jibe at critics of government initiatives while addressing a ‘NaMo for Viksit Bharat’ event in Vadodara.Highlighting the benefits of double-stack container freight trains, PM Modi said a recent service from JNPT in Mumbai to Vadodara carried cargo equivalent to more than 250 trucks.“Recently, a double-stack container freight train was operated from JNPT (Mumbai) to Vadodara—meaning the train ran with one container stacked on top of another. With this single trip, the volume of cargo transported from Mumbai to Vadodara was equivalent to that of over 250 trucks. Now, enter the 'naraaz fufa' figure—the one who will immediately start complaining: ‘What about the truck drivers? Where will the trucks go? What will happen to those who bought trucks?’ Well, 'fufa' has found something to grumble about now,” he said.PM Modi also said the Dedicated Freight Corridor would reduce travel time and logistics costs while saving fuel and benefiting the environment. He said work on the 2,800-kilometre corridor had been completed and that the Eastern and Western Dedicated Freight Corridors were becoming the “backbone” of India's trade and commerce.PM Modi has previously used the “Naraaz Fufa” expression while addressing the centenary celebrations of Delhi University's Shri Ram College of Commerce.At the event, he described critics of government initiatives as people who questioned the need for new projects. Referring to the world's tallest statue, high-speed trains and UPI, the PM said the same “Phoofas” had repeatedly asked what the need for such initiatives was.Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge had also criticised the Prime Minister's remarks at SRCC, saying he was giving the opposition “a new adjective every” year.Kharge listed terms including “Naraz Fufa, Dimaagi Naxal, Urban Naxal, Khan Market Gang, Andolan-jiwi” and “Parjivi”, and accused the government of using such labels while avoiding questions from the youth.The exchange over “Dimagi Naxal” and “Naraaz Fufa” has since added two more expressions to the ongoing political sparring between the BJP and Congress.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: ​In 2015, a California couple bought a distressed 1971 Eichler home at auction; 11 years later, their fully restored house, one of just 15 Eichlers in the area, is asking $2.75M
articles.summary: News News: A rare 1971 Eichler home in San Anselmo, California, has hit the market. The asking price for the four-bedroom midcentury modern house is $2.75 millio.
articles.body: A rare 1971 Eichler home in San Anselmo, California, has hit the market. The asking price for the four-bedroom midcentury modern house is $2.75 million, according to a report by Realtor.com. The home, in the Sleepy Hollow neighbourhood of San Anselmo, underwent a major renovation recently. The 2,537-square-foot property features a unique indoor-outdoor design, modern kitchen, swimming pool, landscaped backyard and smart-home features.Inside the restored midcentury Eichler homeBuilt in 1971 by Joseph Eichler, a famous American builder, this home is a rare abode. There are only 15 Eichler homes in the San Anselmo area at present. Known for their seamless indoor-outdoor living integration, sun-kissed interiors and clean lines, the house also has “expansive floor-to-ceiling glass, sliding doors, open floor plans, and often has radiant heat,” listing agent Kira Swaim of Tam Team at City Real Estate told the outlet.The four-bedroom house was broken when a couple bought it in 2015 from Swaim. Everything in it was broken, quite literally. The pipes were failing, the bones were sound but tired, and almost nothing worked. “It was a distressed sale and was an auction property,” Swaim recalled.But the couple who purchased it had faith. They knew what they were buying, beyond the renovations it needed. Joseph Eichler's tract homes, built between the 1950s and 1970s, remain among the most coveted midcentury residential designs in California. They took care of the renovations while still retaining the architectural beauty of the classic Eichler style.The couple replaced the entire plumbing system, upgraded the windows and doors, and then moved to the spaces where people actually live. The kitchen went through a complete overhaul. “It has all new piping, custom windows and doors; they renovated the kitchen and did a massive project in the backyard to create a camp oasis. There is not much they didn't touch,” the agent told the outlet.Every corner of the house had designer details. The four bedrooms have absolutely bright and airy vaulted wood ceilings with exposed beams. A two-sided fireplace anchored the great room and dining space. Geometric tile and accent walls gave the rooms texture without cluttering them. Vibrant wallpaper throughout added another layer of detail. The retractable glass walls gave direct access to the patio.The kitchen underwent a massive makeover. The bamboo island has expansive cabinetry, high-end appliances, an oversized window overlooking a custom-built entertaining pergola, and sliders that open to the in-ground pool.The previous owners also ensured the house had modern amenities. Solar panels and smart power walls handle the energy side. Fruit and palm trees create corridors of shade.According to the listing agent, who has sold numerous homes in San Anselmo over the years, nothing is quite up to this one.“I have never seen one done to this level,” she added. She also commented on the previous owner, now seller's, incredible taste. “They have an incredible eye for design,” which, according to her, provides a ‘fun, vibrant vibe’ to the house. “It has been a labour of love, for sure,” she said.Swaim says interest has been substantial since listing, with a particular demographic standing out: young families or couples expecting children. And it just makes sense. “Having met most buyers, it appears to live as a primary residence. A lot of families with young kids or kids on the way have looked at it.” The home is also ideal for older adults, given that it is all on one floor.“Sleepy Hollow is a really special community. In the summer especially, kids bike to the clubhouse; there are secret trails and walking paths along the creek. It's kind of like a throwback to childhood memories,” Swaim said.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? Build Your Legacy with TOI Homes.

articles.title: Helsinki is turning the heat from a data centre into warmth for 28,000 apartments; up to 90% of its waste heat is recovered
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Helsinki is finding a practical use for the enormous amounts of heat produced by the equipment running inside data centres. Through a collaboration be.
articles.body: Helsinki is finding a practical use for the enormous amounts of heat produced by the equipment running inside data centres. Through a collaboration between Finnish energy company Helen and telecommunications company Telia, waste heat from Telia’s Pitäjänmäki data centre is being fed into the city’s district heating network. The system is expanding as the data centre grows, with plans for the recovered heat to eventually meet the heating needs of up to 28,000 apartments. At the same time, Telia has increased its waste heat recovery capacity to as much as 90%, turning a larger share of the facility’s previously unused heat into a resource for the city.Helsinki turning data centre waste heat into warmth for 28,000 apartmentsData centres contain thousands of devices that work continuously to process and store digital information. All that equipment generates heat, which must be removed to keep the systems operating safely.At Telia’s Pitäjänmäki data centre, north of Helsinki, that excess heat is no longer treated simply as something that needs to be discarded. Instead, it is recovered and transferred into Helsinki’s district heating network, where it can help warm homes, offices and domestic water.According to Helen, the partnership with Telia has been supplying recovered data centre heat to Helsinki’s properties since early 2023. As the Pitäjänmäki facility expands, it produces more recoverable heat, allowing more energy to enter the district heating system.The recovery capacity has risen dramaticallyThe latest development is the increase in the amount of waste heat that can be recovered from the facility. According to Datacenter Forum, Telia’s recovery capacity was previously about 60%, but the company planned to raise it to as much as 90% in 2025.That means a much larger share of the heat generated by the data centre's equipment can potentially be put to use rather than being lost. The increased recovery capacity has been supported by the expansion of the data centre and the growing number of devices operating inside it.For a city looking for alternatives to combustion-based heating, that makes the Pitäjänmäki facility more than just a place where digital services operate. It also becomes a source of useful heat that is produced alongside those services.Why does the data centre's location matterThe location of the Pitäjänmäki data centre is an important part of the arrangement. Helen says its central position makes it well suited to delivering recovered heat into Helsinki’s district heating network.The system is being developed in phases rather than reaching its full potential immediately. Helen reports that the expanding data centre could initially provide an amount of heat equivalent to the consumption of 14,000 two-room apartments. The longer-term plan is to increase that figure to 28,000 apartments.This gradual approach reflects the connection between the digital facility and the heating network. As the data centre expands and produces more excess heat, a larger quantity can potentially be captured and distributed to homes and buildings.Heat recovery was built into the data centre's designThe idea of using the facility's excess heat was not simply added after the data centre had been completed. According to engineering firm Haskoning, full heat recovery was incorporated into the project from the outset.Haskoning was involved in designing and overseeing Telia’s flagship data centre, which it describes as Finland’s largest shared data centre. The project was intended to support Telia’s ambition to create a highly sustainable and energy-efficient facility while also meeting the security requirements of a shared operation.The design included the equipment needed to move the residual heat into Helsinki’s district heating system, including heat pumps and supporting infrastructure. Haskoning said the project also had to address technical, financial and contractual questions so that the arrangement could work for the different organisations involved.What role does Finland's climate playFinland's relatively cool climate also offers an advantage when it comes to operating a data centre. Datacenter Forum reported that Telia can use cool outdoor air for much of the year to help cool the Pitäjänmäki facility.However, cooling the equipment does not remove the need to deal with the heat it produces. That is where the recovery system becomes particularly useful. Instead of allowing a large amount of that energy to disappear after it has been removed from the equipment, the system captures it for use elsewhere.The approach gives the heat a second purpose. Digital equipment continues doing its primary job, while the warmth generated during that process can contribute to Helsinki's heating supply.A model for reducing combustion-based heatingAccording to Helen, data centre waste heat is an emission-free and stable source of heat that can support its move towards non-combustion-based energy production. The company and Telia have also linked the project to their wider climate goals.The Pitäjänmäki project is also part of Helsinki’s broader experience with using excess heat. Datacenter Forum reported that Helen has been integrating waste heat from data centres into the city's district heating system since 2010.The wider potential is substantial. Helen has separately agreed to connect waste heat from a planned OnZero data centre to Helsinki’s district heating network. According to the Datacenter Forum, that future facility could eventually generate more than 500,000 megawatt hours of heat annually, enough to meet the heating needs of around 70,000 flats, with recovery scheduled to begin in 2027.For now, the Telia project shows how a data centre can serve two different needs at once. While its computers and telecommunications equipment handle the growing demands of the digital world, the heat they produce is increasingly being redirected to the people living and working around them.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Rs 500 notes in kalakand boxes at 1am? Viral video triggers vote-for-cash row in Alwar
articles.summary: ALWAR: A video purportedly showing boxes of kalakand (a local sweet) bearing a photograph of Congress candidate Duleechand Bairwa, along with Rs 500 c.
articles.body: ALWAR: A video purportedly showing boxes of kalakand (a local sweet) bearing a photograph of Congress candidate Duleechand Bairwa, along with Rs 500 currency notes allegedly found inside, has gone viral a day before municipal polling in Alwar.TOI has not independently verified the video.The video is said to be from Ward 42's Diwakari area in Alwar city.According to the visuals, the sweet boxes carried Bairwa's photograph and allegedly contained Rs 500 notes alongside the kalakand.According to locals, a car was seen moving around the Diwakari area at around 1 am, prompting suspicion among residents.As people began following the vehicle, it was allegedly stopped at a corner in the area. The car bore registration number RJ14 CP 6770.Locals alleged that occupants of the car were seen unloading boxes from the vehicle. As a crowd gathered, the occupants allegedly abandoned the car and the boxes and fled the spot.Residents who later opened the boxes claimed to have found kalakand and Rs 500 notes inside.Vaishali Nagar police denied that any such incident had taken place in the area.Congress candidate Duleechand Bairwa dismissed the video as fake, alleging it may have been circulated to defame him ahead of the polls.BSP candidate Sumit Verma, however, alleged that Bairwa was distributing cash in exchange for votes, though the claim has not been independently verified.Reacting to the controversy, Rajasthan forest minister Sanjay Sharma said, "I have seen this video. articles.title: Trump gives Natalie Harp, 2 aides $45,000 each: Why cash gifts for holidays are under scrutiny
articles.summary: US News: US President Donald Trump gave USD 45,000 (about Rs 42 lakh) in cash holiday gifts to three White House aides, including executive assistant Natalie H.
articles.body: US President Donald Trump gave USD 45,000 (about Rs 42 lakh) in cash holiday gifts to three White House aides, including executive assistant Natalie Harp, according to newly released financial disclosures. Another senior aide received USD 20,000 (about Rs 19 lakh).The disclosures were first reported by The Washington Post, which found that the payments were listed as “cash gift for the holidays” in the aides’ annual financial disclosure forms. The USD 45,000 payments went to Harp, communications adviser Margo Martin, and deputy director of Oval Office operations Chamberlain Harris, while Oval Office operations director Walt Nauta received USD 20,000.White House defends Trump’s cash giftsHarp, Martin and Harris each earn USD 150,000 annually, while Nauta’s salary is USD 175,000, according to the White House’s salary disclosure report to Congress.A White House official said Trump has a longstanding practice of giving Christmas gifts to people in his orbit, including employees and aides, both during his time in government and in the private sector.The official said the gifts were unrelated to the aides’ official government duties and were therefore permissible under relevant legal and ethical standards. The White House did not say whether any other staffers received similar gifts.Why the payments have raised questionsThe size of the gifts has prompted scrutiny over federal rules governing additional compensation for government employees.Richard Painter, a former White House ethics lawyer under President George W Bush, told The Washington Post that the payments appeared to raise concerns under a federal law restricting supplementation of federal employees’ salaries.However, former acting Office of Government Ethics director Don Fox said the available facts did not establish that the payments violated the law. He said the circumstances and intent behind the gifts could determine whether they amounted to salary supplementation.Fox nevertheless described the payments as “troublesome”, saying he would feel uncomfortable or beholden to someone who gave him such a large gift.Who is Natalie Harp?Harp, 35, has emerged as one of the most visible aides around Trump. She frequently travels with the president and is known for carrying a portable printer so she can provide him with paper copies of news reports and social media posts.She has worked closely with Trump since joining his staff in 2022 and frequently types his Truth Social posts as he dictates them. Her close relationship with the president has drawn increased attention in recent weeks.Martin has worked with Trump since his first White House term, when she served as a press assistant. She later followed him to Palm Beach, Florida, after his 2020 election defeat and helped run his media operations before returning to the White House after his 2024 victory.Harris serves as deputy director of Oval Office operations and was appointed by Trump earlier this year to the US Commission of Fine Arts, which has oversight of the president’s White House ballroom project.Nauta, a longtime Trump aide and former valet, received the USD 20,000 holiday gift. He was previously charged alongside Trump in the classified-documents case, though the charges were later dismissed.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.summary: India News: The two-day BRICS summit in New Delhi, set to kick-off Saturday, will focus on strengthening cooperation in food and energy security, health, disaster.
articles.body: The two-day BRICS summit in New Delhi, set to kick-off Saturday, will focus on strengthening cooperation in food and energy security, health, disaster resilience and critical supply chains, as member countries seek to build greater resilience amid a fragmented geopolitical environment.The summit, hosted by India under its 2026 chairship, will also cover trade, investment, connectivity and technology, while leaders are expected to exchange views on major global and regional developments.AgendaBuilding resilienceUnder India's resilience pillar, leaders will discuss cooperation in areas including health, agriculture, food and energy security, disaster-risk reduction and critical supply chains. The discussions come against the backdrop of disruptions caused by geopolitical conflicts and growing concerns over the resilience of global supply networks.Trade, investment and technologyStrengthening intra-BRICS trade and investment, improving connectivity and expanding cooperation in high technology will also be among the key economic priorities. India has placed these areas at the centre of its broader effort to deepen cooperation among emerging economies.Global governanceThe summit will also focus on strengthening multilateralism and making global governance more inclusive. The first closed-door session on Saturday is titled “Inclusive Global Governance and Strengthening Multilateralism.”Global and regional issuesLeaders will exchange views on global and regional developments and discuss areas of mutual interest, according to the Ministry of External Affairs.Sunday's main sessionThe main open session on Sunday is titled “Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability: Shaping the Future for Inclusive Global Growth.” The summit will culminate with the release of the New Delhi Declaration.BRICS summit scheduleSaturday (September 12)2:35 pm: Closed-door session for BRICS member countries on “Inclusive Global Governance and Strengthening Multilateralism”.4:25 pm: Leaders will tour the Bharat Innovates Exhibition.5:05 pm: Leaders will assemble at Bharat Mandapam for the family photo, followed by a joint tree-planting ceremony.7:30 pm: Prime Minister Narendra Modi will host a gala dinner for the leaders.Sunday (September 13)9:55 am: Leaders from BRICS member countries, partner nations and outreach invitees will begin arriving.10:35 am: Official group photo.10:50 am: Open session on “Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability: Shaping the Future for Inclusive Global Growth”.The summit will conclude with the release of the New Delhi Declaration.Who is attending?Chinese President Xi Jinping, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, Russian President Vladimir Putin, South African President Cyril Ramaphosa and Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto are among the leaders expected to attend the summit, reported PTI.The summit comes against the backdrop of the global economy facing disruptions from the Russia-Ukraine war, the West Asia crisis, including concerns over the Strait of Hormuz, and the trade and tariff policies of the Trump administration.With the grouping operating on consensus, questions also remain over whether members will agree on a joint statement, particularly amid differences between Iran and the UAE over the West Asia crisis.BRICS originally comprised Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa. The group expanded in 2024 to include Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia, while Indonesia joined in 2025.Belarus, Bolivia, Kazakhstan, Cuba, Malaysia, Nigeria, Thailand, Uganda, Uzbekistan and Vietnam became BRICS partner countries in 2025.The grouping now has 11 member countries, representing around 49.5% of the world's population, 40% of global GDP and 26% of global trade, according to the Indian government.India assumed its fourth BRICS chairship on January 1 this year having previously chaired the grouping in 2012, 2016 and 2021.India's chairship is guided by the theme “Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability”, with a stated focus on a people-centric approach rooted in the principle of “humanity first”.Under India's chairship, more than 350 meetings and high-level engagements have been held across more than 25 cities, covering the grouping's three broad pillars: political and security cooperation, economic and financial cooperation, and cultural and people-to-people exchanges.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: BLA claims 52 Pakistani personnel killed in 28 operations across Balochistan
articles.summary: Pakistan News: The Baloch Liberation Army (BLA) has claimed that it carried out 28 operations across Balochistan between September 1 and 7, killing 52 Pakistani mili.
articles.body: The Baloch Liberation Army (BLA) has claimed that it carried out 28 operations across Balochistan between September 1 and 7, killing 52 Pakistani military personnel and injuring several others.The claims come against the backdrop of separate military operations in the province, with the Pakistani Army saying security forces killed 11 militants in Kharan and Washuk districts on September 6 and 7.According to the Balochistan Post, in a weekly statement, BLA spokesperson Jeeyand Baloch said the group conducted operations in Pasni, Kharan, Kalat, Turbat, Mastung, Surab, Tump, Pishin, Jhal Magsi, Noshki, Chagai and Quetta. The group also said 12 of its rebels were killed during clashes with Pakistani forces.The BLA’s account, as reported by TBP, began with an operation on September 1 at Zero Point in Pasni, Gwadar. The group claimed that it attacked a joint police and Levies post and checkpoints operated by Customs and the Coastal Police, seized weapons and military equipment, and later destroyed the positions.It said an ambush on a convoy at Albat in Kharan and an attack at Garari in Kalat targeted personnel transporting armoured vehicles, with three vehicles severely damaged and personnel killed or injured. On September 2, the group claimed an IED attack followed by an ambush at Guro in Mastung’s Khadkocha area, alleging four personnel were killed and more than seven injured. A day later, it claimed an STOS attack at Hajika in Surab, killing seven personnel and destroying one vehicle.The BLA claimed its Fateh Squad killed 18 Pakistani military personnel and injured five in Pishin’s Ziarat Cross. It also claimed attacks in Tump, Mastung, Kalat and Jhal Magsi, and took responsibility for the killings of Abdul Rehman Langove and Rehmat Saeed in Quetta, alleging both worked for Pakistani forces.Separately, the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), the Pakistani Army’s media wing, said eight militants were killed in Kharan on September 6 after security forces intercepted a group allegedly attempting to block a road. Another three were killed in Washuk the following day, it said.The BLA’s casualty and operational claims have not been independently verified.Meanwhile, TBP reported two fresh alleged enforced disappearances in Balochistan, while five previously missing people had returned home. It said Ali Baloch was allegedly detained by Pakistani forces in Mastung on August 23 and remains unaccounted for.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: In 1904, a Missouri family acquired 15 acres; 106 years later St. Louis County condemned it for Highway 141, and a $238,000 offer became a $2.1 million judgment upheld on appeal
articles.summary: US News: In 1904, a Missouri family acquired 15 acres of land in what is now Chesterfield. More than a century later, St Louis County condemned the property fo.
articles.body: In 1904, a Missouri family acquired 15 acres of land in what is now Chesterfield. More than a century later, St Louis County condemned the property for a highway project, turning the land into the centre of a long legal battle over how much it was worth.The 15-acre tract at 1653 Creve Coeur Mill Road was deeded to Arthur Novel in 1904, according to FindLaw.Arthur and his wife, Stella, lived on the property and operated it as a farm until their deaths. The property had been vacant since 1968 and no house stood there when the county took it.By then, the land was heavily wooded, with a creek, steep bluff and sloping terrain. St Louis County wanted the property for the Page/Olive Connector as part of the extension of Highway 141. The county filed a condemnation petition on December 22, 2009, naming Arthur and Stella’s descendants and their spouses as defendants.The county initially offered $238,000 for the property, according to a 2012 Missouri Lawyers Media report. The family rejected the amount, arguing that the land had greater value because it could be developed for housing despite flood-related restrictions. The dispute eventually reached a jury, which valued the property at $1.3 million.From $320,000 award to a $2.1 million judgmentAfter the condemnation order was issued in February 2010, the owners and the county could not agree on compensation. A court-appointed three-member commission initially awarded the family $320,000.The Novels objected and asked for a jury trial. Before the trial, the commissioners amended their report to state that the family had owned the property for more than 50 years. That became important because Missouri law allowed additional “heritage value” for qualifying family-owned property.The trial took place from December 12 to 15, 2011. The jury awarded $1.3 million for the property. The trial court then added $650,000 in heritage value, equal to 50% of the jury’s fair market value finding, along with $158,769 in prejudgment interest.That brought the judgment to about $2.1 million. The county appealed, challenging the amount as well as several decisions made during the trial.Family and county disagreed over the land’s valueThe family’s appraiser, Ernest Demba, used the comparable-sales approach to value the property. He said its highest and best use was residential villa development, pointing to nearby Mill Ridge and Terra Vista developments.Demba valued the Novel property at $2 per square foot. The 15 acres covered 648,373 square feet, putting his valuation at $1,296,746.Demba did not use a Terra Vista transaction as one of his three comparable sales because the land had sold for only 30 cents per square foot. He said the transaction involved non-money consideration and was not a true market sale.The county challenged Demba’s testimony about Terra Vista and information concerning changes to the land’s flood designation. However, the Supreme Court noted that the county had itself questioned Demba extensively on those issues and had not properly preserved its objections.The family’s lawyer, Robert Denlow, described the trial as an explanation of how the land could potentially be developed.“We basically gave the jury a mini-course on how to be a developer using 15 acres of floodplain and floodway with a creek running through it,” Denlow said, as quoted by Missouri lawyers media.The county argued that development would be legally difficult and expensive. County Counselor Patricia Redington also objected to testimony about the family’s attachment to the property.“The constitution calls for just compensation, and just compensation means fair market value, not sentimental value,” Redington said.Supreme Court rejects county’s challengesThe county also challenged testimony about a possible $496,000 settlement figure. A county employee testified that Arthur Novel had said he would settle for that amount during an earlier commissioners’ hearing.But the trial court concluded that the figure represented a settlement position, not Novel’s opinion of the property’s fair market value. The Supreme Court agreed that the trial court could accept or reject the testimony and noted that settlement negotiations are generally protected from being used as evidence.The county also challenged limits placed on testimony from two Chesterfield employees, civil engineer Jeff Paskiewicz and planning director Aimee Nassif. The trial court allowed them to explain general development requirements but did not allow them to give undisclosed, property-specific opinions.The Supreme Court upheld that decision, saying the county had not disclosed such opinions during discovery.$1.3 million verdict upheldThe county argued that the jury’s $1.3 million award was excessive. The Supreme Court rejected the claim.Demba’s calculation came to $1,296,746, which he agreed was close to $1.3 million. The court said the jury had reasonably rounded the figure and that the testimony of a single qualified expert could provide substantial evidence supporting the verdict.The court also rejected the county’s constitutional challenge to Missouri’s heritage-value law. Under the law, property held by the same family for at least 50 years could receive an additional 50% of its fair market value when a taking prevented substantially the same use.The Supreme Court held that the law did not replace the constitutional requirement of fair compensation. Instead, it provided additional compensation. It also ruled that determining heritage value did not improperly interfere with the jury’s role because the jury decided the property’s fair market value, while the additional statutory amount was determined by the judge.The Missouri Supreme Court ultimately affirmed the trial court’s judgment, leaving the family with an award of about $2.1 million for the property taken for the Highway 141 project.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Trump claims firefighters lifted him to safety near ground zero after 9/11: What facts show
articles.summary: US News: President Donald Trump recounts a dramatic 9/11 story about being rescued by firefighters. However, evidence of his presence at Ground Zero remains unconfirmed, raising questions about his claims as the 25th anniversary approaches.
articles.body: President Donald Trump has described a new version of his experience after the September 11 attacks, claiming two firefighters lifted him to safety because they feared a nearby building was about to collapse.Trump made the claim Tuesday at a White House event honouring first responders ahead of the 25th anniversary of the attacks. He said he had taken workers from a construction project he was overseeing to the area shortly after the attacks.According to Trump, he was near the "US Steel" building when people feared it could come down. He said two firefighters then grabbed him under the arms and carried him away."They grabbed me under the arms, said, 'Gotta get out of here,'" Trump said. "And they literally lifted me up. This is not easy to do. I'm big. They lifted me up and they started running with me."There is no public evidence establishing that Trump was inside the building he referred to, known today as One Liberty Plaza, when the incident took place.In an earlier version of the story in 2016, Trump said the firefighters helped him "a couple of days" after the attacks. In a social media post on Tuesday night, he clarified that he was not at the site on September 11 itself but said he was there "shortly thereafter".Trump's account has also previously been questioned by Richard Alles, a retired New York Fire Department deputy chief who spent months at the World Trade Centre site after the attacks. In 2019, Alles told The New York Times that he had never seen Trump at Ground Zero."I spent many months there myself, and I never witnessed him," Alles said. "He was a private citizen at the time. I don't know what kind of role he could have possibly played."There were, however, documented concerns about the stability of buildings around Ground Zero in the days after the attacks. One Liberty Plaza was evacuated on September 12 after fears that it could collapse, although officials later determined that the building was structurally sound. Rescue workers were also moved away from the area during another alert on September 14.Trump has previously described being involved in the recovery operation at Ground Zero, including claims that he sent a large group of workers to help. Those accounts have been disputed by people who were involved in the response.The White House did not provide evidence when asked to substantiate Trump's latest account. In an email to CNN, it said that Trump was a private citizen at the time and that "not everything he did was documented".White House spokesperson Davis Ingle later accused the media of trying to use Trump's remarks to attack him, saying the president had been describing his experience of New York in the aftermath of the attacks.Trump later said on Truth Social that "everything I said was exactly accurate".His latest account comes days before the 25th anniversary of the attacks, when Trump is expected to attend a commemoration at the Pentagon rather than Ground Zero in New York.Trump also used Tuesday's event to honour the family of Welles Crowther, a volunteer firefighter who died after helping people escape the South Tower. Crowther became known as the "man in the red bandana" because of the red bandana he wore over his face while assisting survivors.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: ‘Wanted to teach him a lesson’: Accused on assault that killed Manipuri musician
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: The men accused of killing Manipuri musician Chongtham Vikram Singh in southeast Delhi allegedly wanted to “teach him a lesson” for objecti.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The men accused of killing Manipuri musician Chongtham Vikram Singh in southeast Delhi allegedly wanted to “teach him a lesson” for objecting to noise outside his home, but did not expect the assault to turn fatal, police said on Wednesday.During questioning, the accused allegedly told police that they assaulted the 54-year-old musician with fists and blows after he objected to the commotion outside his residence in Kilokari, according to the police, as cited by news agency PTI.Singh had on some occasions complained to the owner of a nearby dhaba about the noise caused by people gathering there, a senior police officer said. However, police had not received any formal complaint from Singh regarding the noise.The dhaba remained open until around midnight and attracted customers from neighbouring areas as well as students living nearby, police said.Police examine racial angle, dhaba owner’s rolePolice said they were examining all aspects of the case, including whether there was any racial angle. So far, the investigation has not revealed any instance of a racial slur being used against Singh during the altercation, a police source said.The FIR registered at Sunlight Colony police station on the complaint of Singh's son mentions Section 103(2) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, pertaining to group murder in circumstances covered by the provision.Police are awaiting the post-mortem report to ascertain the exact nature of the injuries sustained by Singh. Prima facie, he appears to have suffered internal injuries that led to his death.The police are also examining the role of the dhaba owner and its operations. So far, no irregularity in the functioning of the establishment has come to light, sources said. Action would be taken against the owner if anything emerges during the investigation.CCTV footage is being scrutinised and witnesses are being questioned to establish the sequence of events and the circumstances that led to the assault.Singh died hours after assaultThe incident took place around 11.30 pm on Sunday when Singh went downstairs after hearing a commotion outside his home.According to the complaint, when his son heard his father shouting, he opened the door and saw a group of men kicking and punching him.Singh subsequently returned upstairs but complained of breathlessness. His 20-year-old son Yaiphaba took him to Holy Family Hospital, where he succumbed to his injuries around 6 am the following day, police said.Seven men have been arrested and a juvenile apprehended in connection with the case. The accused have been identified as Bharat Kumar, 19, Pramod, 26, Ramzan Khan, 22, Deepanshu, 21, Mohan Vishwakarma, 32, Vijay, 36, and Mannu, 26.Northeast body seeks swift, impartial probeThe killing has sparked concern among members of Delhi's northeastern community, with several residents alleging that people from the region face racial slurs and discrimination in the national capital.The North Eastern Students' Organisation (NESO) on Wednesday condemned Singh's killing and demanded a swift and impartial probe.NESO chairman Samuel B Jyrwa said the incident was deeply disturbing and called for all those responsible to be brought to justice.“It is deeply disturbing that a person can lose his life merely for raising an objection to disturbance outside his own home. We demand a transparent and impartial investigation and exemplary punishment for every person found responsible,” Jyrwa said in a statement, as cited by PTI.Jyrwa said the killing could not be viewed in isolation from what he described as continuing harassment, racial discrimination, stereotyping, intimidation and violence faced by people from the Northeast in different parts of mainland India.“For years, Northeastern citizens living, studying and working outside the region have repeatedly reported being subjected to racial slurs, verbal abuse, physical attacks, social discrimination and other forms of humiliation because of their appearance, identity and place of origin,” he alleged.NESO urged authorities to treat the matter with seriousness and urgency and ensure that nobody responsible for the crime evades accountability.“The law must be applied firmly and equally, irrespective of the identity or background of the perpetrators,” Jyrwa said.The organisation also called for stronger preventive measures, effective enforcement of the law, sensitisation of police and public institutions, and mechanisms to ensure the safety and dignity of people from the Northeast.“The loss of Chongtham Vikram Singh is not merely a personal tragedy for his family and loved ones, but a matter of deep concern for the entire Northeastern community,” Jyrwa said.Who was Chongtham Vikram Singh?Singh had lived in Kilokari for more than two decades. He was a well-known musician and guitarist, and had been the lead guitarist of the Manipur rock band Phoenix in the early 1980s.He later worked as a music teacher and performer in Delhi.NESO expressed solidarity with Singh's family and the people of Manipur and demanded justice for him and accountability for everyone found responsible for his death.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Built in 1917, a 22-bedroom Washington hotel was run by one family for 50 years; now this century-old building is listed for just $195,000
articles.summary: News News: A historic 22-bedroom hotel in Washington that sat vacant for years is now on the market for less than $200,000. Built in 1917, the ‘landmark’ buildin.
articles.body: A historic 22-bedroom hotel in Washington that sat vacant for years is now on the market for less than $200,000. Built in 1917, the ‘landmark’ building with lots of potential is waiting for someone bold enough to take on its future. The Palace Hotel in Odessa, which once thrived as a family enterprise, is now listed at $195,000, according to a report by Realtor.com.The property commands attention not because of what it is now, but because of what it once was and what it can become. The structure spans 4,572 square feet across three levels, with the kind of craftsmanship that is now vanishing from modern construction and architecture. The building features original millwork, a grand staircase, built-in cabinetry, oversized windows and wood panelling throughout. All of these would cost far more to recreate from scratch.Once a family-run businessFor nearly 50 years, one family took care of the Palace Hotel through its best years. It's unclear exactly when that operation ended or how long the building has sat vacant, but the gap has certainly taken its toll. The asking price of the property also reflects this reality. This is certainly a project property, not a turnkey investment.The layout gives clues about its past life. The formal living and dining rooms anchor the ground floor, while a kitchen and eat-in area sit nearby; all of these were practical spaces designed for feeding guests. The second level of the building is packed with bedrooms and balconies to maximise guest capacity. The third floor offered more of the same. A lower-level summer kitchen was also built for occasional entertaining and large gatherings.The building retains much of its original layout. It’s a historic structure that has survived 107 years with its fundamental design untouched. The property is certainly a project to work on, but offers endless opportunities. It’s ideal for property flippers betting on sweat equity. Or a boutique hotelier with a vision for restoration. Someone dreaming of a large single-family home with more space than they know what to do with. An entrepreneur who sees conference centre or event space potential.Beyond the price tag, there’s work that needs to be done. Though the main structure remains intact, the building is in need of significant updating. The windows need attention, as do the systems.The new owner can either restore, redevelop or completely transform the building into a residence or workplace. With the right resources and, of course, patience, the Palace can become something extraordinary.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? Build Your Legacy with TOI Homes.

articles.title: Salvadoran TPS deadline nears, impacting 200,000 immigrants
articles.summary: The Temporary Protected Status designation expires Wednesday, but the statute does not give a specific time for when that happens.
articles.body: MIAMI — Temporary legal protections for about 200,000 immigrants from El Salvador expire Wednesday, but the statute does not give a specific time for when that happens. On Wednesday a Department of Homeland Security spokesperson said in a statement to NBC News, “An announcement on El Salvador’s TPS will be made at the appropriate time. Until such announcement is made, Salvadoran individuals present in the U.S. under TPS retain protection.” The Trump administration has ended protections for hundreds of thousands of TPS recipients from Venezuela, Haiti and other countries. If DHS takes no action, protections are automatically extended for six months. This rare reprieve happened in May, when the protections were automatically extended to about 11,000 Lebanese, allowing them to stay and work in the U.S. for another 180 days. About 200,000 people from El Salvador have lived in the U.S. since 2001 under TPS, which allows people already in the country to remain with work permits for renewable periods of up to 18 months, if the secretary of Homeland Security determines conditions are unsafe for return. They are eligible for work permits. During President Donald Trump’s second term, Homeland Security has ended TPS for more than 1 million people from 14 countries, including El Salvador, Venezuela, Haiti, Honduras, Nicaragua, Afghanistan and Syria. Only about 103,000 from three countries remain protected with termination dates in October for Ukraine and Sudan, and November for Lebanon. The Trump administration obtained a major victory when the Supreme Court ruled in June that Homeland Security acted within its authority by ending TPS for about 350,000 Haitians and 6,000 Syrians. The impact of the decision extends far beyond Haitians and Syrians, potentially affecting nearly 1.3 million people from 17 countries on TPS. Congress created temporary protections in 1990 TPS was created by Congress in 1990 to prevent deportations to countries suffering from natural disasters or civil strife. It was granted to El Salvador following two devastating 2001 earthquakes that left hundreds of thousands of people homeless. Just before leaving office, President Joe Biden extended TPS for El Salvador for 18 months to Sept. 9, 2026. The vast majority of Salvadoran TPS holders have children born in the U.S. Many have lost their jobs and fear being detained, separated from their American family members, and deported to a country they barely know. El Salvador has been a Trump ally El Salvador, once one of the most violent places in the world, has become one of the safest countries in the Americas since Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele ordered mass arrests in 2022. In April 2025, the State Department upgraded El Salvador’s travel advisory to its highest level, citing a drop in violent crimes and murders. Bukele has been an ally of Trump’s policy of mass deportations and was one of the first countries to receive deportees and held them at a mega prison in El Salvador also known as CECOT. Human rights groups and advocates have denounced mass and arbitrary arrests, torture, and disappearances in the Central American nation’s prison system. Trump received Bukele at the White House in April of 2025 and invited him to participate in a military coalition to fight against drug trafficking and organized crime. Less than a year later, in July of 2026, Trump and Bukele met again in Washington, the Salvadoran president has not publicly stated whether he requested an extension of TPS from the Trump administration. In 2019, during the first Trump administration, Bukele asked Trump to extend TPS. It remained because there were lawsuits. Salvadorans in the U.S. sent $9.9 billion in remittances to El Salvador last year, representing 24% of country’s gross domestic product, according to El Salvador’s central bank.

articles.title: Passenger killed after train hits truck at Poland level crossing
articles.summary: It is the second such incident in Poland in days and the prime minister says tough new regulations are needed.
articles.body:
A passenger has been killed in Poland as a train derailed after colliding with a concrete mixer truck at a level crossing.

About 120 people were on board the intercity train at the time of the crash in Sokolniki Suche, some 100km (60 miles) south of the capital Warsaw, at around 11:20 (09:20 GMT). PKP Intercity, the country's national long-distance rail operator, said: "20 people were injured, including four seriously".

It is the second such incident in days in Poland.

Prime Minister Donald Tusk said the accident was "very serious and also means that we must immediately begin urgent work on tougher regulations".

Tusk said the "radical toughening of the rules" was needed "for those who, unfortunately, quite systematically drive on to level crossings despite the barriers and red lights".

Reports from the scene say there were traffic lights at the level crossing of Wednesday's accident and the cement mixer had hit the carriage behind the train engine.

It is still too early to determine the sequence of events.

However, Deputy Infrastructure Minister Piotr Malepszak has said that the driver of the truck - who is among the injured - had said "he was blinded by the sun".

Last week, a lorry driver crossed the first set of barriers at a level crossing as they were closing and dramatic footage showed him reversing, then moving forward in an unsuccessful attempt to evade another PKP train which was coming at speed.

articles.title: 'It's been a nightmare': Passengers face airport chaos after UK air traffic issue
articles.summary: Thousands are still stranded as people describe sleeping on floors and "carnage" in baggage reclaim halls.
articles.body:
Passengers left stranded by an hours-long air traffic control issue at UK airports have told the BBC of nightmare delays, chaotic scenes and waylaid holiday plans.

Hundreds of thousands of people are thought to have been hit with flight cancellations and delays throughout Tuesday and Wednesday after a technical problem caused the air traffic outage.

That included newlyweds Sasha and James, who told BBC Your Voice they spent three hours stranded in Wetherspoons at Gatwick after their flight to their honeymoon was cancelled.

Some also described sleeping on airport floors and chaos at baggage reclaim as thousands looked to reorganise their plans, while others have been stranded abroad while trying to get back to the UK.

Nats, the UK's air traffic control provider, has said flight operations are now stable but airlines have warned of continued knock-on disruption. Passengers have been advised to check their flight status before travelling to airports.

The boss of Nats Martin Rolfe apologised for the disruption and also met with Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander on Wednesday, who asked for a full investigation.

Most of the UK's main airports were hit by the problem including Heathrow, Gatwick, Luton and Glasgow.

Speaking to the BBC earlier on Wednesday, newly married couple Sasha and James Graham said they were boarding their flight from Gatwick to Funchal on the island of Madeira when they were "turned right back around".

Sasha said: "We spent three hours stranded in Wetherspoons, making the best of it.

"It's certainly not the experience we planned, but I think starting your marriage with a national disruption is certainly very memorable!"

They weren't able to reclaim their luggage but have since booked onto a new flight.

"It feels like we will spend our honeymoon at Gatwick," Sasha added.

Phil White also spoke of incredibly busy scenes in the airport's baggage reclaim hall, describing it as "carnage" as an influx of disrupted passengers tried to find their luggage.

"All the bags from every cancelled flight were sent to one reclaim carousel. So there were a thousand or so people trying to get close enough to get their cases," he said.

"The baggage hall was the worst and they're very lucky that there wasn't any sort of incident as tempers frayed and the concourse was getting hotter."

Elsewhere, people spoke of spending the night on the floors of airports and hotels across the globe when flights back into the UK were cancelled.

Sukie Perera, from Cardiff, describing her experience of being stuck in Turkey said "it has been a nightmare" and communication at the airport was poor.

She won't be able to fly home until Thursday but joked that at least "the view is beautiful".

Paul Willows, currently in Rhodes, Greece, with his family said they had to sleep on the floor of a hotel's conference room on Tuesday night.

He said: "They stripped all the cushions off the sunbeds and laid them in the conference room. I dare say there were about 80 of us on the floor."

Despite it having "not been a comfortable night at all", Paul said there was a "good element of pulling together" from those impacted.

Alan Jones and Kelly Fewery also said their family was "absolutely exhausted" after sleeping on the floor of Dalaman Airport in Turkey without blankets or pillows.

More than 340 flights were cancelled on Wednesday, according to aviation analytics company Cirium.

Airlines are still obliged to get passengers to their destinations - even if that is via another carrier - when their flight is cancelled, or give a refund.

Those delayed may have the right to food, or a hotel stay, depending on the length of the wait. But no extra compensation payments should be expected as the air traffic control issue was not the fault of any airline.

articles.title: Europe's royalty pay respects to King Harald V in Norway
articles.summary: The Prince of Wales and three Nordic kings were among those who attended proceedings on Wednesday.
articles.body:
Dozens of European royals and heads of state, including the Prince of Wales and three Nordic kings, have paid their last respects to King Harald V in Oslo.

Thousands of people lined the route during a funeral procession from the royal palace to Oslo Cathedral on Wednesday afternoon, nearly two weeks after the king died aged 89.

After the ceremony and burial, the Norwegian royal family, including the new King Haakon, his wife Queen Mette-Marit, and his mother and Harald's widow Queen Sonja greeted crowds from the palace balcony.

A minute's silence was also observed throughout the country. Harald, who was seen as a popular, modernising figure, was on the Norwegian throne for 35 years.

After 13 days of national mourning, the day began on Wednesday with ceremonial troops assembling at Akershus Fortress, the medieval castle where Harald was later laid to rest.

A procession then took place, with Haakon, his sister Princess Märtha Louise and his children Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra and Prince Sverre Magnus, following the late king's coffin on foot.

Mette-Marit, who recently underwent a successful lung transplant , and Sonja, 89, followed in a car.

Prince William, representing his father King Charles III , attended the funeral alongside the Princess Royal, who was there in a personal capacity as godmother to Norway's new monarch.

They were among 30 royal figures from Sweden, Jordan, Monaco, Belgium, Spain, Japan and Denmark.

Among the non-royal heads of state attending the funeral were Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier along with five foreign prime ministers.

During the funeral service at the cathedral, Mette-Marit was seen wiping her eyes, as Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre delivered a eulogy, saying Harald had struck "a balance between being stately and down-to-earth and that he had "made Norway greater".

Queen Sonja, who was also visibly emotional during the ceremony, laid a red rose on Harald's coffin.

A poignant moment as three bell tolls marking the end of a minute's silence in the cathedral was briefly interrupted by a mobile phone alarm going off.

The day after his death, his son Haakon VIII thanked him for "being such a good dad" and said he had "always stayed true" to his values and commitments.

Royal observers have described the late king as well respected and beloved, and who was seen as a "grandfather" of the nation.

In the final months of his life, he and his family had faced personal challenges and scandal.

Earlier this year, documents revealed Mette-Marit's frequent contact with Jeffrey Epstein. She later said she wished she had never met the late sex offender.

Meanwhile, her son, Marius Borg Høiby - who is not a royal figure himself but grew up within the family - was given a four-year jail term for two counts of rape in June .

Høiby, who is under house arrest pending appeal, was granted permission to attend the funeral, and sat in the second row during the cathedral ceremony alongside Märtha Louise's children.

At the end of the service, four F-35 fighter jets flew over the cathedral in a "missing man" formation.

Harald's casket was then carried in a procession to the Palace Chapel at Akershus Fortress, where a private ceremony was attended by family members, foreign royals and other guests including the country's prime minister.

King Harald was laid to rest there alongside several members of the royal family, including his father King Olav V, his mother Crown Princess Märtha, and his grandparents, King Haakon VII and Queen Maud.

Norwegian flags across Oslo were raised from half mast to the top to mark the end of the burial, while the royal family returned to the royal palace.

In a display of gratitude for the support they had received since the king's death on 28 August, the family - Haakon, Mette-Marit, Ingrid Alexandra, Sverre Magnus and Sonja - then appeared on the balcony to greet tens of thousands of people who had gathered outside.

articles.title: Lichfield man who created indecent AI images of girls jailed
articles.summary: Lewis Davison, from Lichfield, is jailed for two years and two months after images were reported.
articles.body:
A man used artificial intelligence (AI) platforms to create indecent images of women and girls, Staffordshire Police said.

Lewis Davison, 26, from Litchfield posted a series of AI-generated pornographic images on closed Telegram groups.

In some captions on the social media messaging app, he called for the women depicted in the images to be raped and assaulted, investigators found.

He was jailed for two years and two months after pleading guilty at Stafford Crown Court on 27 August.

Davison's devices were seized and he was arrested after the images were reported to Staffordshire Police.

He was charged with eight counts of publishing an obscene article and one count of permitting the taking of a pseudo-photograph of a child. He admitted all of the charges.

PC Matthew Asbury, who dealt with the investigation, said : "I'm pleased we've been able to apprehend Davison and stop him from causing further harm to women and girls online."

He added: "This type of crime can have a profound impact on victims and I can assure the local community that we will take every possible step to make sure those responsible are brought before the courts as quickly as possible."

Davison has also been placed on the sex offenders register for 10 years.

articles.summary: Jimmy Kimmel returned from a long hiatus by taking aim at FCC Chair Brendan Carr, referencing his show's suspension and the ongoing clash over free speech.
articles.body: Late-night host Jimmy Kimmel took aim at Federal Communications Commission (FCC) Chairman Brendan Carr during his show on Tuesday, returning from a summer break, and said, "We are still here." The late-night host noted that Tuesday's episode of "Jimmy Kimmel Live!" was its 4,000th episode. "We’ve done 4,000 of these. Which is, it’s a lot of shows," Kimmel said. "According to the White House, it’s too many shows." ROSIE O'DONNELL WON'T WORRY ABOUT FCC, BRENDAN CARR AHEAD OF KIMMEL HOSTING, DOESN'T 'PAY ANY HEED TO THEM' "There are those who said we would never last this long. There are even those who used the regulatory might of the FCC to unconstitutionally try to make sure we didn’t last this long. But we did it the hard way, Brendan. And we are still here," Kimmel said. Kimmel referenced his show's brief suspension and ongoing clash with Carr in 2025. FCC BOSS BRENDAN CARR MAINTAINS EARLY ABC LICENSE RENEWAL IS ABOUT DEI PROBE, NOT JIMMY KIMMEL CONTROVERSY JIMMY KIMMEL SUGGESTS CHARLIE KIRK ASSASSIN WAS ONE OF THE ‘MAGA GANG’ DESPITE REPORTS OF LEFTIST LEANINGS The FCC did not immediately return Fox News Digital's request for comment. White House spokesman Davis Ingle told Fox News Digital in a statement, "Jimmy Kimmel is a no-talent loser who has be-clowned himself with tanking ratings and by spewing disgusting lies to his dwindling audience. He is so devoid of actual talent that nobody with any commonsense would ever watch him unless it was to laugh at his miserable failures." Carr warned ABC and Disney in September 2025 that the FCC could take action over comments made by Kimmel about the man accused of assassinating Charlie Kirk on Sept. 10, 2025. "In some quarters, there's a very concerted effort to try to lie to the American people about the nature … of one of the most significant newsworthy public interest acts that we've seen in a long time in what appears to be an action by Jimmy Kimmel to play into that narrative that this was somehow a MAGA or a Republican-motivated person," Carr said at the time. "Look, we can do this the easy way or the hard way. These companies can find ways to change conduct, to take action, frankly, on Kimmel, or, you know, there's going to be additional work for the FCC ahead," Carr continued. KIMMEL SEIZES ON TRUMP'S OLD AGE JOKE DURING MEETING WITH KING CHARLES, JOKES HE 'SHOULD BE FIRED FOR THAT' Kimmel's comment from Tuesday's show was likely referencing Carr's "hard way" remarks from 2025. Kimmel also took aim at President Donald Trump during Tuesday's episode, saying he accomplished nothing all summer. "You know, Donald Trump and I have one thing in common: We both accomplished nothing all summer long," he said, criticizing inflation, Trump's approval numbers, the reflection pool and the war in Iran. Kimmel said, "At this point, Blockbuster Video has a better chance of reopening than the Strait of Hormuz." REMEMBERING CHARLIE KIRK: TURNING POINT USA'S ANDREW KOLVET REFLECTS ON CONSERVATIVE GROUP'S CHALLENGING YEAR Kimmel was briefly suspended last year over remarks he made about the man accused of assassinating Kirk. Iger said Kimmel was asked to apologize, saying, "We just wanted him to acknowledge that it was an ill-timed and probably inappropriate comment." articles.title: Attacks on journalists spiked ahead of Saxony-Anhalt election
articles.summary: The campaign in the lead-up to regional elections in the German state of Saxony-Anhalt was marred by a high number of attacks on the media, the dju journalis...
articles.body:
High number of attacks on media reported during campaign leading up to regional elections in Saxony-Anhalt.

Far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party in Saxony-Anhalt falls just short of absolute majority in elections.

Tensions and assaults on journalists documented in Saxony-Anhalt ahead of closely watched elections.

The campaign in the lead-up to regional elections in the German state of Saxony-Anhalt was marred by a high number of attacks on the media, the dju journalists' union reported on Wednesday.

Sunday's elections in Saxony-Anhalt, to the west of Berlin, were closely watched around the world, as they looked likely to produce the first far-right state government in Germany since World War II.

However, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party fell just short of an absolute majority, garnering 43.8% of the vote, but still far ahead of the conservatives of Chancellor Friedrich Merz.

Tensions ran running high in the lead-up to the vote, with the dju documenting 46 assaults, intimidation and serious obstruction targeting media workers since May.

"What we are witnessing in Saxony-Anhalt is a systematic attempt to suppress critical public opinion," said Lucas Munzke of the Verdi trade union, the umbrella organization that includes the dju.

By contrast, Reporters without Borders recorded five attacks on media workers in Saxony-Anhalt in all of 2025.

articles.body: Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic dissolved parliament on Wednesday and called snap parliamentary elections for October 25, bringing forward a vote that was originally scheduled for next year.According to Reuters, the election comes after nearly two years of anti-government protests in Serbia, sparked by the November 2024 collapse of a railway station awning in Novi Sad that killed 16 people."Were the elections necessary for us if there were no such ​tensions, if there were no such political conflicts, certainly they would not be necessary," Vucic said in a televised statement. He added that ​any delay in the election "would threaten the survival ⁠of democracy."Vucic has been Serbia’s dominant political figure since 2014, serving as either president or prime minister. He was prime minister from 2014 to 2017 before becoming president.His ruling Serbian Progressive Party nominated him on Saturday to run for prime minister in the October election. It remains unclear whether Vucic will resign as president before the parliamentary vote.The student-led protest movement, which has organised some of Serbia’s largest demonstrations in decades, has not yet said whether it will support a candidate or political bloc.Pollster CRTA said the election would test support for Vucic after months of anti-government protests, while his political opponents face a difficult challenge in the vote.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
