articles.title: Bridget Phillipson sets up 'class unit' as social mobility advisers ditched
articles.summary: The equalities minister says the move will bring government efforts to tackle disadvantage "in-house".
articles.body:
The government is to scrap its advisory body on social mobility, with a new "class unit" charged with improving life opportunities for poorer people.

The move will see the abolition of the Social Mobility Commission (SMC), responsible for advising ministers on tackling inequality in England.

Equalities Minister Bridget Phillipson argued the move would bring the government's efforts to tackle disadvantage "in-house".

But the commission's outgoing chair Alun Francis criticised the decision, adding that class was a "messy concept around which to organise policy".

Previously known as the Social Mobility and Child Poverty Commission, the body was renamed in 2016 when the Conservative-Liberal Democrat coalition government scrapped legally binding child poverty targets.

Since then, its remit has been confined to promoting social mobility in England more broadly and publishing an annual report, alongside advising ministers.

Phillipson said her move to scrap the body, which comes amid wider efforts to cut the number of arm's length bodies in Whitehall, would redirect resources from "oversight to direct delivery" of the government's goals.

"This decision marks a pivotal step in embedding a focus on socio-economic inequality into the heart of government," she said in a statement.

Speaking to BBC Radio 5 Live, she said there had been a "squeamishness in talking about class" and it was a "big area that's been missing" in policy formation.

But Francis, who became the commission's permanent chair in 2023, accused ministers of failing to engage with the body on its plans and said he had seen "no detailed plan" for how the new unit should be assessed.

In a statement, he added that the name of the unit posed "obvious problems of definition" and "risks being deeply patronising, to equate being working class with being disadvantaged".

He also took issue with a government press release that said there were no examples since 2016 of its work having directly informed government policy, arguing it had influenced plans for clean energy jobs and the "devolution agenda".

The government said the new unit would sit within the Office for Equality and Opportunity, alongside existing teams responsible for covering race, sex, LGBT and disability rights contained in anti-discrimination laws.

It added that the unit would be responsible for introducing a new legal duty for public bodies in England to consider how their policies affect those on low incomes.

Detailed work on the duty has been ongoing since last year, following a commitment from Labour in its 2024 election manifesto.

The duty, dubbed "Harman's law" after it was written into the Equality Act by former Labour equalities minister Harriet Harman, was never enacted under the coalition government and has effectively remained dormant in England ever since.

It has applied in Scotland and Wales since 2018 and 2021 respectively, however, whilst a number of public bodies in England have adopted it voluntarily.

In July, the government said the new duty in England could apply in areas such as education, health, and housing, although the full scope of the policy, as well as guidance on how it would apply, is yet to be set out.

The Conservatives have vowed to scrap the duty if elected, with shadow equalities minister Joy Morrissey saying it would "drag businesses and public bodies into yet more bureaucracy" and "encourage class warfare instead of aspiration".

articles.title: Indian-origin billionaires lead US immigrant rich list: Who are Forbes 2026’s latest entrants?
articles.summary: US News: India leads the Forbes 2026 list of immigrant billionaires in the US with 19 entrants, highlighting the success of Indian-origin business leaders. Key figures include Vinod Khosla, Hemant Taneja, and Shyam Sankar, emphasizing tech's role in wealth accumulation.
articles.body: India has emerged as the biggest birthplace of billionaire immigrants living in the United States, with 19 Indian-origin business leaders featuring on Forbes’ 2026 ranking of the country’s richest foreign-born citizens.The number marks an increase from 12 Indian-born billionaires on last year’s list, with seven new names joining the ranking. The new entrants include General Catalyst chief executive Hemant Taneja, Palantir chief technology officer Shyam Sankar and Astera Labs co-founders Sanjay Gajendra and Jitendra Mohan.Israel and Taiwan followed India, with 11 immigrant billionaires each.Among the Indian-origin names, Sun Microsystems co-founder Vinod Khosla ranked highest, with an estimated fortune of $13.9 billion. He was the 13th richest immigrant billionaire overall, while Tesla chief executive Elon Musk topped the ranking and Google co-founder Sergey Brin also placed ahead of him.Other prominent billionaires on the list include Zscaler chief executive Jay Chaudhry, IndiGo co-founder Rakesh Gangwal and software entrepreneur Romesh Wadhwani.Microsoft chief executive Satya Nadella and Alphabet chief executive Sundar Pichai also retained their places among the wealthy foreign-born citizens living in the US.Technology continued to be a major source of wealth for the new Indian-origin entrants. Taneja, who heads General Catalyst, was valued at $3.6 billion, with the firm’s investments in artificial intelligence companies, including Anthropic, contributing to the growth of his fortune.Sankar, who joined Palantir’s leadership as its chief technology officer, also entered the billionaire ranking as the company’s valuation and influence have grown.The 2026 ranking includes a record 144 immigrant billionaires living in the US, with a combined wealth of $2.2 trillion. Last year, 125 foreign-born billionaires on the list had a combined fortune of $1.3 trillion.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: CIA chief Ratcliffe may take bigger role in stalled Russia-Ukraine talks
articles.summary: US News: CIA director John Ratcliffe is preparing to take a larger role in US efforts to negotiate an end to the Russia-Ukraine war, as the Trump administratio.
articles.body: CIA director John Ratcliffe is preparing to take a larger role in US efforts to negotiate an end to the Russia-Ukraine war, as the Trump administration looks to revive a diplomatic process that has stalled without a breakthrough.The Financial Times, citing five people familiar with the plans, reported that the White House is considering reducing the role of US special envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who have been central to the negotiations. The possible change has not been finalised by President Donald Trump.Ratcliffe's potential involvement would bring the head of the US intelligence agency more directly into the peace effort. He could take part in shuttle diplomacy between Moscow and Kyiv and maintain contacts with Russian and Ukrainian intelligence officials. Ratcliffe recently travelled to Moscow and met Russian intelligence officials, giving him a separate channel for discussions with the Kremlin.The move comes as the US-backed negotiations have struggled to make progress. The biggest obstacle remains the gap between Moscow and Kyiv over the terms of a potential settlement, particularly territory and security guarantees.Russia has continued to demand territorial concessions from Ukraine, including areas of the Donbas that Moscow claims. Ukraine has rejected giving up territory as part of a peace agreement. Kyiv has also sought strong security guarantees to prevent another Russian attack after any ceasefire or settlement.Moscow, meanwhile, has shown little indication that it is prepared to abandon its core demands. Recent discussions have therefore failed to narrow the differences between the two sides. The US negotiating effort has also faced criticism over the limited progress made during successive meetings.The latest attempt to revive the process involved Witkoff and Kushner travelling to Moscow and Kyiv for meetings with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy. While the talks kept diplomatic channels open, they did not result in a major breakthrough.The process has also been affected by Washington's shifting priorities, with the Trump administration's attention increasingly focused on other international crises. That has made it harder to maintain sustained diplomatic pressure on Moscow and Kyiv.Russia has said it remains open to resuming US-mediated talks, but the fundamental disagreements remain unresolved. The Kremlin has continued to insist that the underlying causes of the war must be addressed, while Ukraine wants a settlement that preserves its territorial integrity and provides long-term security.Against this backdrop, Ratcliffe's possible expanded role could signal an attempt by Washington to bring a different approach to the negotiations. His intelligence background and contacts with Russian officials could give the US another channel to assess Moscow's position and explore whether there is room for movement.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Osama bin Laden had Taliban rival assassinated 2 days before 9/11 attack
articles.summary: Pakistan News: Ahmad Shah Massoud, the prominent Afghan resistance leader and one of the Taliban's strongest rivals, was assassinated on September 9, 2001, just two .
articles.body: Ahmad Shah Massoud, the prominent Afghan resistance leader and one of the Taliban's strongest rivals, was assassinated on September 9, 2001, just two days before the 9/11 attacks, in a killing believed to have been ordered by al-Qaeda chief Osama bin Laden as a favour to his Taliban hosts, according to a Newsweek report.Massoud, who led Afghanistan's Northern Alliance, was killed while being interviewed at his camp in the Panjshir Valley by two men posing as Belgian television journalists. The two al-Qaeda operatives had concealed explosives inside a video camera despite undergoing security checks before meeting the resistance leader, Newsweek reported.The Northern Alliance did not officially confirm Massoud's death until September 15.Massoud had built a powerful insurgent network in northern Afghanistan and remained a major obstacle to Taliban control of the country. His influence and popularity also made him a key figure among forces opposed to the Taliban.According to Newsweek, bin Laden was believed to have ordered Massoud's assassination partly as a favour to his Taliban hosts and partly because he expected the United States to launch retaliatory strikes following the planned September 11 attacks.Eliminating Massoud was also strategically important because bin Laden understood the Afghan leader's value as a military commander and political figure who could have played a significant role in any campaign against the Taliban and al-Qaeda.The assassination alarmed the CIA, which had maintained contacts with Massoud and other Afghan opposition figures.Gary Berntsen, the CIA officer who later led the agency's first team into Afghanistan after the 9/11 attacks, recalled that the news "made me feel sick to my stomach ... I figured this was the end of the Northern Alliance."CIA director George Tenet was less pessimistic, noting that the agency had maintained relationships with other Afghan warlords.Tenet later wrote, "Masood's [sic] brutal murder by al-Qaeda on the eve of the 9/11 attacks might have undone our plan before it got under way if we hadn't maintained contact with other warlords in the north."Tenet's meeting with Pakistan's ISI chiefOn the day Massoud was assassinated, Tenet was having lunch with Pakistani Gen. Mahmood Ahmed, then head of the Inter-Services Intelligence (ISI), Pakistan's main intelligence agency.According to Tenet's account, he pressed Mahmood on al-Qaeda and Taliban leader Mullah Omar. Mahmood assured him that Omar wanted what was best for the Afghan people and suggested that the CIA try bribing key Taliban officials to secure bin Laden's surrender."As gracious as he could be over the lunch table, the guy was immovable when it came to the Taliban and al-Qaeda," Tenet later wrote.Mahmood would be in Washington on September 11, when he met senior US lawmakers including Senate Intelligence Committee chairman Bob Graham, House Intelligence Committee chairman Porter Goss and Senator Jon Kyl.In the aftermath of the attacks, Mahmood held further meetings with US officials as Washington pressed Pakistan to cooperate in its campaign against terrorism. US military forces were also clandestinely deployed to Pakistani territory as the Bush administration prepared its response to the attacks.Massoud's assassination therefore came at a critical moment. Two days before the attacks that transformed US foreign policy and triggered the war in Afghanistan, one of the Taliban's most formidable opponents had already been eliminated.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
